Literature:
Theodore E. Stebbins, Jr., The Life and Work of Martin Johnson Heade: A Critical Analysis and Catalogue Raisonné, New Haven, 2000, p. 333, no. 535, illustrated.

Lot Note:
While his fellow contemporaries of the Hudson River School only specialized in one genre, Heade was unique in devoting equal attention to both landscape and still life painting throughout his long career. He first started painting floral still lifes during his stay in New York City in 1858. Although he was mostly known for his landscapes at the time, his floral subjects received high praise from critics, the Boston Transcript reporting: "At Williams and Everett's may be seen floral pieces by Heade [that] are remarkably truthful, and betray a most careful and earnest study of nature. They are the best specimen of flower painting ever seen."

Heade painted several types of flowers. Although critics are still unsure of the artist's original intentions through his choices of specimens and vases, he seems to have favored roses. Similarly to George Lambin, "the other great rose specialist," Heade enjoyed depicting the flower's subtle hues of red and delicate petals. In the 1870s, he started to simplify his work, and focused on the very dramatic Général Jacqueminot rose, a wild flower characteristic for its brilliant quality.

The present work highlights the artist's departure from earlier sophisticated themes, and his yearning for simpler compositions. Here, Heade depicts six beautiful red rose stems on a bare table top, which is delicately covered by luxurious gold velvet. The flowers, all isolated from their natural environment, shine against an austere black background. The true subject of the painting is therefore not the branches themselves, but rather the effect of the warm light on the surfaces and textures of the leaves, blossoms and shiny drapery, thanks to careful and deliberate composition.

Heade used this floral composition as a prototype which he would then use over and over in a series of rose paintings, similar to what he did with his scenes of marshes and orchids.

Literature:
Rick Stewart, The American West: Legendary Artists of the Frontier, Dallas, 1986, p. 18; p. 19, illustrated.

Lot Note:
Baltimore painter, Alfred Jacob Miller, produced a compelling visual record of the western fur trade after receiving a significant 1837 commission from Captain William Drummond Stewart, a Scottish patron. Miller traveled with Stewart to the annual fur traders' rendezvous, a vital trade meeting in the Green River Valley of present-day Wyoming. This exchange, facilitated by the American Fur Company, brought together diverse groups, including American mountain men and members of several Native American nations such as the Sioux, Cheyenne, and Crow, allowing them to acquire necessary provisions in exchange for furs. Miller's observational "trail sketches" from the journey became the source material for numerous oil and watercolor paintings, notably a series of 200 oils and watercolors commissioned by William T. Walters in 1858.

These works, delivered with descriptive texts over the next two years, provide not only a detailed visual history but also a window into the prevailing 19th-century biases of the artist and explorer. Miller’s commentary on Schim-a-co-che describes him with equal parts admiration and prejudice, comparing his dignity to that of a "civilized gentleman" while juxtaposing the chief's distinction with "common Indians." The present lot, the creation of which coincides with Miller's output from his travels with Drummond, is part of an invaluable yet historically complex document of this period in the colonization and exploration of the American West.

Literature:

Ace Powell Art Galleries, Inc., Studies in Bronze by A. Phimister Proctor, an exhibition catalogue, Kalispell, 1975, p. 14, another cast illustrated.

Lot Note:
Alexander Phimister Proctor solidified his reputation as a premier sculptor of the American West with the creation of Pursuit of the King of the Herd. Ever sensitive to the artistic landscape, he elected to interpret a high-drama buffalo hunt even after contemporaries like Charles Marion Russell had already secured widespread recognition for similar compositions. For the present work, Proctor recruited the noted Nez Perce rider, Jackson Sundown, nephew of Chief Joseph, as his primary model. Sundown was a celebrated public figure, renowned equally for his achievements in the rodeo circuit and for his near-mythic survival tactics while mounted during conflict. Proctor’s journals detail his fruitful collaboration with Sundown and document how his model would ride and maintain demanding poses repeatedly, allowing the sculptor to capture the precise anatomical and human details of the hunt.

The resulting bronze is a tour de force of Proctor's command of form and ability to translate kinetic force into static material. The sculpture commemorates the climactic moment of the chase, where the hunter leans perilously across his mount to pierce the massive, churning bulk of the buffalo. The composition is a study in counterpoint, pitting the sheer weight and wild desperation of the cornered bison against the streamlined thrust and controlled aggression of the hunter and his leaping horse. The figures appear frozen, momentarily suspended above the ground in a high-stakes battle for self-preservation–for both hunter and hunted. Pursuit of the King of the Herd, much more than a depiction of a classic Western trope, embodies a universal narrative of skill, conflict, and survival.

Lot Note:
Few American painters active in the second half of the 19th century so effectively captured the sea and surf in oil–whether luminous, crashing, raging, stormy or calm, from Grand Manan to Nantucket to Cornwall–as William Trost Richards. While unidentified, the subject of the present painting may well be Rhode Island, possibly Newport, where Richards first summered and built his home, or Conanicut Island overlooking Narragansett Bay, the site of his cliff top home "Gray Cliff." While Richards more commonly worked on a smaller scale than he has in Rolling Surf (including in the case of his watercolors), the quality and detail of his larger format seascapes do not disappoint. Here the canvas is roughly divided in half between a cumulus cloud-filled sky and choppy green sea, with a wave about to crash at left and a lone seagull swooping above rockery at right. Painted towards the end of Richards's life, the painting underscores the artist's adherence to the "truth to nature" philosophy espoused by John Ruskin and the Pre-Raphaelites in the which vistas are depicted in a detailed, unvarnished manner rather than the romanticized approach favored by the Hudson River School painters, who sought to evoke the sublime in their depictions the American landscape.

Lot Note:
While Troye was the premier American thoroughbred horse painter of his day, the present painting was a result of his trip to the Middle East accompanied by the wealthy Kentucky horseman, Alexander Keene Richards. Troye travelled there in search of Arabian horses. During this sojourn from 1855-1856, "Troy would execute some of his most famous works, careful renditions of some of the sites in the Holy Land most sacred to Christianity, thereby departing from his usual practice of animal portraits in favor of landscapes." (Gary A. O'Dell, "Artist in the Holy Land: The Pilgrimage of Edward Troye," Cheiron: The International Journal of Equine and Equestrian History, vol. 5, no. 1, 2025, p. 88). The present painting, and another mural-sized canvas, Syrian Ploughman (1856), comprise Troye's foray into Orientalism. Here we see a bazaar in Damascus before the entrance to the Great Mosque, centered by an Albanian officer astride a white mare called "Lulie" (O'Dell, ibid., p. 94). As Claudia Pfeiffer notes in describing this painting, "It is easy to get lost in the rich colors, vibrant details, and the individual animal and figurative portraits in the highly-detailed composition."

Lot Note:
About the present lot, Mary Lublin writes: "The young American certainly absorbed Bonnat's preference for large-scale portraiture and direct, unpretentious presentation of the model. L'Italienne, also known as At the Fountain (1875) was Pearce's first full-scale figure subject. This portrayal of a studio model dressed in an Italian peasant costume, standing beside a stone fountain, presented the type of sentimental peasant genre subject prevalent at the Salons of the 1860s and 1870s. Its compositional elements recall Bonnat's Girl by a Fountain (1875, Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York) from the same date, in which a barefoot peasant girl tries to drink from an outdoor fountain. The Bonnat was said to have been a subject commissioned by American socialite and collector Catherine Lorillard Wolfe, reputedly the richest woman in America, which would have provided an additional incentive for the determined pupil. Pearce may have also remembered William Morris Hunt's enthusiasm for Jean-Baptiste Corot's melancholic Italian models in ethnic costume. While L'Italienne lacks the complexity of pose and handling of Bonnat's work, the composition ignores the anecdotal in favor of a more direct experience of the sweet young model."

She continues, "When the painting was shown at the Philadelphia Centennial in 1876, the critic for the New York Times complained it was 'the life school again,' but acknowledged that there was 'a look at it.' Pearce's emphasis on expression and demeanor, as well as a palette that was described as 'rich without being obtrusive' and his 'naturalistic rendering of textures' reveal a glimpse of the more mature artist." (A Rare Elegance: The Paintings of Charles Sprague Pearce, New York, 1993, p. 11)

Lot Note:
Painted in 1893 at Giverny, Playing with Jimmy captures a tender domestic moment between Butler’s wife, Suzanne Hoschedé-Monet—Claude Monet’s stepdaughter—and their infant son, Jimmy Butler. With its brilliant palette and interlocking geometric design, the work stands among the artist’s most refined explorations of light, color, and form.

The composition reveals Butler’s deep engagement with both French Impressionism and the emerging decorative modernism of the Nabis. He orchestrates a rhythmic interplay of curves and planes—the vase of flowers, the mother and child, the table and mirror—creating a luminous pattern that transforms everyday intimacy into pictorial harmony.

As noted by Richard R. Love (Theodore Earl Butler: An American Impressionist, Chicago, Chicago, 1985, pp. 131-132, pl. A), this canvas represents a pivotal moment in Butler’s evolution, anticipating the spatial abstraction later pursued by Bonnard and Vuillard.

A rare fusion of American warmth and French sophistication, Playing with Jimmy is a masterwork of Butler’s early Giverny period, and an affectionate family portrait that also marks a turning point in his modernist vision.

Lot Note: Rendered in warm hues and heightened with areas of broken brushwork, the present painting is a wonderfully rendered composition that is pleasing to the eye and exemplary of a familiar Miller subject–a beautiful and fashionably dressed young woman seated before her dressing table and facing left to right in profile with sunlight streaming through a window behind her. The famed American Impressionist's canvases engage and draw in the viewer, and were, according to Miller himself, "not for the staid environment of museums, but for the comfortable intimacy of people's homes." Such paintings were meant to be "...decorative, the conveying of a pleasant optical sensation." There are many related paintings by Miller in which a well-dressed young woman either sits before a mirror, or as in the present work, holds a mirror. The viewer's eye is drawn to the young woman's face, then down to the mirror she delicately holds at an angle in her left hand, then over to her right hand drawn upwards across her chest and over her necklace, resulting in a sort of compositional counterbalancing which adds to the work's visual appeal.

It would be hasty to assume that The Mother is simply a straightforward depiction of motherhood and nothing else. Although the woman and her child occupy the majority of the composition, the eye is immediately immersed into the fabric of her dress displaying an intricate floral arrangement, a subject Maria Oakey Dewing excelled at painting. The dress, with its abundantly flowing design and myriad folds and recesses that take the viewer on a winding, seemingly never-ending tour, invites us to look closely at Dewing’s rich aesthetic, and compels us to recognize the artist in the woman portrayed here.

Through an interplay of uniform, darker tones and eclectic, brighter hues, the painting indeed signals an uneasy ambivalence between Dewing’s maternal self and her artistic identity. By the time the present painting was executed in 1905, Chase had long established himself as one of America's leading portraitists. Lot Note:
Storytelling is an integral part of Howard Pyle’s artistic practice. A successful illustration does not merely capture a moment; rather, it encapsulates its unfolding, hinting at what preceded it and what might ensue. Here, Pyle dramatizes the June 28th, 1778 Battle of Monmouth, a momentous episode in the American Revolutionary War, at a time when George Washington was losing support from his army as Commander-in-Chief and needed a victory to inspire his fellow compatriots and boost the momentum the fledgling nation required to flourish.

More than a century later, when Pyle executed this painting, historians knew that the Battle of Monmouth had a rather inconsequential outcome and did not, in fact, see Washington unequivocally victorious. But Washington and the Continental Army did capitalize on the fact that they did not cede ground to the British Army, and the battle still became, in the collective psyche, a landmark episode.

The scene portrayed here, imbued with heroism and grit, subscribes to this narrative, borrowing visual elements typically found in epic tales. The vertical composition is anchored by the stern figure of the soldier raising his sword, readying to deal a last and fatal blow to the enemy, with an exhilarated infantry in the background. The medium of the grisaille, with its sharp focus, furthers the event’s significance, fixing in paint not just a moment in time, in the manner of a snapshot, but the very spirit of the nation.

The flagpole towering over the gathering is metaphorically extended through the friar’s gaze pointed downward to the abundant fruit exhibited on the indigenous tapestry covering the ground, hinting at the above-mentioned dual agenda. The towering postures of both Cortes and Montezuma may suggest a stand-off, but the power struggle is clearly uneven, with Cortes firmly stepping on the carpet, indicating a move to appropriate the goods presented to him. Montezuma is standing by, closer to the edge of the canvas, not only conveying submission, but also an ominous sense of gradual disappearance.

Lot Note:
Albert York, a self-taught artist who shunned celebrity and was perpetually dissatisfied with his work, has nonetheless gained steady recognition as a groundbreaking, if somewhat elusive, figure in 20th century American Art. His paintings are characterized by strikingly economical means and methods, including broad, swath-like brushwork, palette uniformity, as well as flat and pared-down forms. This apparent simplicity, however, is cleverly challenged by myriad nods to seminal themes and techniques gleaned from aesthetics of past decades and centuries, indicating that York’s practice was quite intentional.

Girl in Rowboat echoes the Impressionist focus on ease and leisure, depicting a relaxed young woman amidst a verdant landscape. Lush as it is, however, the scenery is deserted, stressing the figure’s solitariness, a motif previously explored by American Realists such as Edward Hopper. And by blending support and medium, York calls attention to the materiality and artifice inherent in artistic representation and subscribes to a key Modernist tenet. The saturated green hues interlock effortlessly with the deep brown shade of the board intermittently showing beneath the painted surface, simultaneously activating and suspending disbelief. Indeed, just as the painting draws the viewer in, it also gives away its illusory quality. York further blurs the line between the real and the imagined, the organic and the artificial by suffusing the painting with discordance in gentle but unmistakable ways. Perhaps most unsettlingly, the rowboat sits on grass rather than the body of water visible just behind it, a visual legerdemain reminiscent of Magritte’s Surrealist paintings.

All of these seemingly innocuous incongruities seep the painting in quiet uncertainty. A barely perceptible yet inescapable unease emerges from the sun-dappled, carefree, blithely uneventful moment depicted here, like an elicited feeling or underlying mood rather than an outright statement. This perhaps works as a commentary on artistic practice, in keeping with York’s rejection of trends and straightforward categorization, a reckoning that art, an inherently vain undertaking, cannot fully encapsulate the breadth and depth of human experience. Lot Note:
The paintings of Jessie Arms Botke, particularly her captivating representations of birds, holds a distinguished position in the narrative of early California art. Botke's approach capitalizes on her training at the Art Institute of Chicago, her extensive international travels, and her far-reaching professional engagements. Following an influential European tour in 1909, Botke settled in New York, where she honed her skills as a tapestry designer and interior decorator for Herter Looms. Her commissions, which included murals featuring avian subjects for actress Billie Burke and San Francisco's Hotel St. Francis, solidified her enduring passion for birds. The decorative use of white peacocks in Burke’s residence was a pivotal moment; Botke described this initial encounter with the birds as "love at first sight."

After establishing her home in California—first in Carmel-by-the-Sea in 1919 and later in Santa Paula, just north of Los Angeles—Botke dedicated the balance of her long career to depicting the region's rich ornithological subjects. She favored pale-plumed species such as swans, herons, and, most famously, peacocks, often placing them within lush, almost theatrical settings.

In the present lot, Peacock on Fountain, a magnificent white peacock perches amidst richly colored, autumn-hued foliage. The bird's voluminous train streams down, its delicate, lacy texture contrasting beautifully with the large, graphic leaves of what appear to be chestnut or buckeye trees. The composition's lower register reveals a stately, formal garden setting with a line of classical statues flanking a pathway leading toward a distant clearing. This arrangement—where the natural world dominates the foreground and a constructed, architectural landscape provides the backdrop—speaks to Botke's ability to merge decorative formality with naturalistic splendor. Her appreciation for the design element in these creatures is evident; the white peacock’s form lent a simple, yet beautiful white silhouette against a darker ground, with the texture of the tail providing complexity without sacrificing the bold clarity of the pattern.

Lot Note:
The year 1917 was a time of creative momentum for Charles Burchfield, whose early prolific output helped establish him firmly as a groundbreaking participant in American Modernism. At the time, Burchfield still lived in his childhood home in Salem, Ohio. The house—and by extension the scenery around it—has been credited for inspiring and fostering his aesthetic development. Burchfield himself referred to that period of his career as his “golden year,” and curator Henry Adams went as far as calling the dwelling “the most important house in American art history,” because of the high volume of works associated with it.

Watertower and Queen Anne’s Lace is an exceptional example of Burchfield’s early work produced in Salem, straddling the line between Regionalist tendencies and Modernist aspirations. It reveals Burchfield’s concern for industrial expansion and its impact on local rural landscapes. At the same time, it already highlights Burchfield’s whimsical take on landscape painting with the distinct organic and wispy forms that have become visual signifiers of his aesthetic. Here, the vegetation in the foreground, velvety, rounded, and plump, clashes with the angular, sprawling, and towering factories in the middle ground. But the stark visual contrast between the natural and the industrial is softened by the smoke billowing into the sky, bulbous and cottony, endowing the scene with a sense of wholeness, in spite of the jarring elements Burchfield assembled together.

Lot Note:
In the twilight of his career, Bellows underwent a noticeable evolution of style and subject matter, transitioning from dynamic representations of urban life and sporting events to an exploration of the landscape. Risley's Pig House depicts the environs of Woodstock, New York, where Bellows spent part of every year from 1920-1924 and where, according to art historian, Bruce Weber, the artist found a perfect complement of “nature and neighborhood.”

Executed in 1924, the present lot is an unsentimental study in vernacular architecture. The composition is anchored by a tightly clustered group of farm buildings, dominated by the striking, rust-red central house and the dark, imposing mass of a barn to the left. The vermilion of the central structure–the titular pig house–is offset by the cool, metallic blue-green of its corrugated roofing. This juxtaposition and the work's palette align Bellows with the exuberance of Fauve and Expressionist-inspired modernists, whose work he would have encountered as co-organizer of the landmark 1913 Armory Show.

The strength of Risley's Pig House is rooted in its unrestrained, assertive brushwork. The angular wooden fencing of the pigpen provides strong diagonals that direct the viewer’s eye into the picture space, establishing a sense of enclosure and emphasizing practical, utilitarian geometry. The right foreground is particularly animated, built up with thick, gestural strokes of earthy brown and gray impasto, suggesting the texture of the mud and overall “mood” of the yard. Bellows's approach is one of immediacy and, indeed, of modernity, elevating the site–a humble farmscape–to a well-orchestrated collision of light, color, and form.

Lot Note:
Romare Bearden started experimenting with the collage medium in the 1960s and by the end of the decade, it had become ubiquitous in his practice. The early 1970s also coincided with significant recognition from the art world with several important exhibitions of his work. Concerned with the African American experience and the Civil Rights movement more broadly, Bearden sought to instill elements of ritual, spirituality and tradition into contemporary depictions of Black life.

The present work, portraying a nude woman accompanied by a dove, is an explicit reference to the Greco-Roman myth of Aphrodite/Venus. But the bird also signals a connection to the spiritual realm, evoking of the magic often associated with conjure women. The stark verticality of the work reinforces the ethereal feel of the composition, hinting at a beyond, or an escape toward the social justice African American artists like Romare Bearden championed through their art. Here, Bearden intertwines Western mythical traditions with ancestral and enduring African rituals to offer an allegorical glimpse at the rich, complex, and multiform experience of African Americans, a cultural palimpsest echoed by the thoughtful assembling of paint and paper at work in a collage.

Lot Note:
The paintings that Milton Avery produced in the Gaspé Bay are rare. Oxcart is no exception, having sold directly from the artist’s studio in May 1940 to The Valentine Gallery in New York.

The Gaspé landscapes are significant as they represent a critical moment in the artist’s career, when Avery began to use color as his primary means of expression. Its structural function is reflected in the restricted, darker palette in the foreground, in which Avery channels the art of Pablo Picasso and George Braque to set the emotional tone of the scene–a difficult act of labor under the beating summer sun. In contrast, the sky and sea are set in striking blue and green tones, which elevate the overall composition and give it a sense of reverie and quietude.

Following in the Cubists’ footsteps, Avery reinterprets a traditional pastoral scene as a two-dimensional arrangement of forms, tones, and textures–all simplified. The slightly skewed perspective reinforces the flatness of the pictorial space, allowing Avery to achieve his signature synthesis between realism and abstraction, making Oxcart a quintessential piece of his 1940s production.

Above all, the work reflects Avery’s attachment to the landscape, specifically the New England seaside along Gloucester, a place he first visited in 1920 and often returned to between then and 1945 with his wife Sally. The sea held a profound meaning for Avery throughout his life. "We were followers of the sea,” Sally Avery reminisced. “On the beaches of Provincetown, Gloucester and Gaspé we braved the surf and rocky shore, spending endless hours contemplating the sea...Always the sea beckoned, at times with figures, at times with boats. But it was the sea, alternately black and mysterious or ruddy and gay that expressed the mystery and independence that makes its lure unfathomable. For Milton this was a subject to challenge again and again.” Here, the emerald-green sea occupies much of the composition. It enlivens it and acts as a literal pool of reflection and contemplation; it hints at a metaphorical space beyond, which contrasts with the prosaic scene in the foreground.

Lot Note:
Sumac Lane is characteristic of the paintings Daniel Garber produced in the late 1920s, when he frequently depicted small dwellings, secluded paths, and modest towns gently enfolded by the natural world. Painted in December 1928 from the top of the hill at Point Pleasant, Pennsylvania, the scene overlooks the quarries on the distant shore of the Delaware River. It is the second in a series of at least three paintings (including Ferry Road, cat. no. 518) that feature the same solitary “warm grey house” looking down Sumac Lane, and belongs to one of the earliest groups that Kathleen Foster has described as forming “the finest achievement of his career.”

The composition is intentionally understated: the soft horizontal strata of the quarry in the distance are set against the elegant vertical sweep of the bare tree in the foreground, creating a subtle tension between stability and movement. The house sits quietly among winter grasses and sumac, its snow-capped roof catching the pale seasonal light. Garber revisited this site later in his career, most notably in the winter of 1930, adding a bare tree at the far end of the house and illustrating the compositional liberties he was willing to take in shaping his landscapes.

When exhibited at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in 1929, paintings of this homespun simplicity resonated with audiences eager to define American art in plain, unpretentious terms. Through his meticulous study of winter light and the rugged contours of the Bucks County terrain, Garber elevates an ordinary hillside dwelling into a vision of serenity and quiet majesty. As Sam Hunter observed, and as Sumac Lane so beautifully demonstrates, Garber (much like George Inness before him) was able to draw “from the spectacle of nature an elevating and ennobling experience, in a somewhat melancholy, elegiac mood.”

Lot Note:
Shad Fisherman No. 2 exemplifies a key moment in John Fulton Folinsbee’s transition from Impressionism toward a bolder, more uninhibited strain of Modernism. While firmly rooted in the observed reality of riverside labor in his beloved Pennsylvania, the painting transcends pure representation to achieve what Folinsbee increasingly sought in his mature work: a synthesis of modernist execution with Impressionist sensitivity conveyed through atmosphere, color, and the interplay of light. Indeed, and as Kirsten Jensen aptly observes, “the real subjects of Shad Fisherman No. 2 are light—the stark contrasts between the looming clouds and the summer sky—and the moody anticipation of the storm to come."

The fishermen, quickly sketched in a strokes, were among Folinsbee's favorite subjects. Although they add a bit of human activity, here they merely serve as a means to cast the various effects of the light, some blinding white while others blend with the blue-shadowed casting net, thus heightening the drama of the coming storm. Here, Folinsbee departs from the more linear construction of his earlier industrial landscapes, which marked his first attempts at Modernism, and instead orchestrates a swirling vortex of movement, using sweeping brushwork and intensified tonal contrasts to accentuate the dramatic effect of the moment, thus underscoring the emotional power of what appears to be, at first glance, a very mundane activity.

Shad Fisherman No. 2 is emblematic of Folinsbee’s finest works from the late 1930s in that it embodies the artist’s deepening engagement with Modernist ideas, particularly the atmospheric mysticism championed by Arthur Bowen Davies, whom Folinsbee deeply admired (alongside Robert Henri), and whose landscapes Duncan Phillips praised for their affinities with Cézanne and El Greco. The darkened palette, heightened shadow-play, and compressed composition in the present work all reflect this influence, transforming the scene of shad fishing into an eternal, almost mythical American life tableau, which would led contemporary art critic Edward Alden Jewell to hail Folinsbee as “one of the lords of impasto, who can swing his brush with an authority that is boisterous but that seldom falls short of capturing the effect desired.”

Lot Note:
Contrary to other fellow Pennsylvania Impressionists who spent the early years of their career in France like Edward Redfield (1869-1965) or Daniel Garber (1880-1958), Fern Coppedge almost never travelled outside of the United States. In the summer of 1925, however, at the age of forty-two, the artist embarked on a two-month trip to Europe and visited Italy for the first time, stationing in Florence.

Coppedge's introduction to the Tuscan landscape stimulated an important change in her palette, which started incorporating bolder hues, and in her style, which embraced simplified, flatter shapes. The present work is a view of the Arno river from the artist's hotel balcony in Florence, which Coppedge executed from memory a year after her return to the United States. In a later interview, Coppedge recalled how inspiration struck her: "From my hotel, overlooking the Arno in Florence–looking from the balcony window–I saw the Arno River flowing gently like molten gold. It was late afternoon, and lazy Italian boatmen floated past in the dark, sturdy barges, winding their way down the river. Along the opposite bank were charming old stucco houses in colors of pale and rusty yellow, rose, pink, and old red. Tiled roofs, arched doorways and deeply recessed windows, balconies, towers and turrets against the background of cypress trees-all mirrored in the waters of the Arno. Church towers and ancient castle walls patterned against the hills inspired me and thrilled me with an irresistible desire to put on canvas my impressions."

Florentine Gold is similar in composition to The Golden Arno, another important work by the artist now in the collection of the New Hope-Solebury (Pennsylvania) School District, and which received numerous positive comments when it was exhibited in the landmark "Philadelphia Ten" show of 1926.

Pigeon Cove depicts a harbor in Rockport, Massachusetts, a recurring source of inspiration for Fern Coppedge, who summered there on numerous occasions. The work displays many of the hallmarks of Coppedge’s style, including a bold, colorful palette and soft draftsmanship, converging to yield a picturesque rendering of a familiar setting. Shown at sunset and at a high angle perspective, the painting offers a definite sense of depth, dramatizing an otherwise uneventful scene. Yet, it also suggests intimacy, the quaintness of the view transcending the implied vastness of the body of water and landscape on the horizon. Following the path of the sailboat making its way back, soon to anchor for the evening, the eye quickly travels from the distant shore to the marina to finally close in on details such as the shack on stilts or the gulls circling above—details that we notice precisely because of the local color and sense of authenticity they provide. Coppedge indeed excelled at capturing atmospheres emanating from expansive vistas and her rendering of locales is rooted in what makes them homelike.

Lot Note:
Born in Summit, New Jersey in 1876 and trained at Columbia University’s School of Architecture, Colt initially joined a New York architectural firm before abandoning the discipline altogether, eager to escape what he once described as the restrictive demands of “clients’ tastes or whimsies.” Drawn instead to the freedom of artistic expression, Colt settled at Phillips’ Mill, where he formed a close friendship with William Langson Lathrop, Edward Willis Redfield, Daniel Garber, Charles Rosen, Rae Sloan Bredin, and Robert Spencer–the first generation of New Hope School painters. Though he pursued painting, design, and crafts with equal devotion, Colt is remembered today primarily for his luminous Impressionist landscapes, which he composed in the studio because of a chronic heart condition that prevented prolonged outdoor study.

The present painting stands apart within the limited corpus of Colt’s work. The largest known oil by the artist, it represents one of his most ambitious surviving compositions ever to appear on the market. On the monumental canvas, Colt inscribes a now-vanished chapter of life along the Delaware River with an almost cinematic immediacy. Rather than offering a distant vista, Colt brings the viewer directly onto the river, where the diagonal movement of a barge contrasts gently with the horizontal (and echoing) banks as well as the rustling canopy of trees overhead. A figure stands at the stern, pole in hand, while a team of mules waits at the riverbank; small yet evocative details that anchor the composition in lived history. In this sentimental view, Colt memorializes the everyday labor and quiet poetry of river life before mechanization transformed the region’s rhythms forever.

Colt’s brisk, shimmering brushstrokes animate the reflections on the river’s surface, while the bright, sun-filled palette envelops the entire composition in a sense of warmth and pastoral calm. The canvas resonates with nostalgia, not only because it preserves a nearly forgotten mode of transportation, but because Colt renders it through a screen of dappled light, mirrored water and soft atmospheric haze, which transforms the industrial subject into an homage to the enduring beauty of Bucks County.

Colt died suddenly of a heart attack in 1926, leaving many canvases unfinished and an even greater number tragically destroyed by subsequent occupants of his home. This historic loss makes the reappearance of the present canvas on the market even more exciting and momentous.

Lot Note:
Daniel Garber’s career as a painter can be distilled as a heartfelt celebration of Bucks County—of its hilly topography, humbly quaint architecture, and slow-paced rural lifestyle. The tight composition of Solebury–Springtime, centered on the stone buildings surrounded by burgeoning trees and deep green grass, conveys the close bond between man and nature, the fact that, in Bucks County, life is inextricably tied to the land.

Garber emphasizes natural simplicity as the source of bliss, eschewing the rapid changes brought about by urbanization and industrialization. The scene is bathed in warm sunlight, the nascent springtime evoking rebirth and even the perpetuation of a flourishing way of life established from time immemorial. The motif of the sheep in the foreground and the raw stone of the barn on the left further the notion that simplicity is indeed the antidote to a tiresome and overwrought lifestyle.

But Garber’s celebration of simplicity is not limited to symbolism. His painting, in a very formal dimension, is in fact a feat of artistry, at once concealing and illuminating artifice, only to make his point about simplicity even starker. The three figures, immersed in both scenery and conversation, appear completely oblivious to the viewer, and by extension, to the fact that they are objects of contemplation, just like the artwork they inhabit. Here, Garber acknowledges his craft, the inherently designed nature of his landscape, while simultaneously suggesting that it is not exactly what is worthy of our attention. Instead, what we are compelled to recognize is the simple, authentic, idyllic—devoid of unnecessary artifice—quality of the place that the three figures also embrace and embody.

Lot Note:
Executed just a year before his passing, the present canvas reflects the final phase of experimentation that marked the artist’s late career. During this period, Spencer began to loosen the disciplined, almost pointillist precision of his earlier work and embraced a freer, more deconstructed touch. Although his subject matter remained largely consistent (he continued to revel in scenes of people working, playing, and simply moving through urban space), by 1926 he had begun to look beyond Bucks County, traveling through Europe and New York, and at times even inventing entire cityscapes from scratch, as appears to be the case here.

In Vacant Lot, the dappled brushwork and heightened lime greens introduce a renewed chromatic richness, recalling the freshness of his early Impressionistic canvases. Yet the atmosphere is quiet, even slightly rigid; the open field and placid light soften the scene, while the severe row of tall tenements anchors it with a stark urban weight. Buildings that were once minutely detailed are now reduced to broad, generalized forms, outlined masses with only the faintest suggestion of detail. This simplification extends to the figures as well. Faceless and understated, those in the foreground are rendered with swift, economical strokes, as though the artist were testing how few marks were needed to suggest presence. At the right, the figures dissolve into dabs and flicks of pigment, their forms barely held together by contour and gesture.

Although Spencer publicly rejected abstraction, these late works resonate with the broader modernist impulse of the 1930s to pare down the visible world to its essential rhythms. The result is an image both experimental and profoundly human. Unlike many of his fellow New Hope School painters, Spencer retained a deep attachment to the human figure, filtering his sympathetic vision of everyday life through an increasingly spontaneous and immediate touch.

Lot Note:
This evocative late painting by Robert Spencer captures the artist at a moment when his long-standing fascination with humble architecture, working communities, and riverfront industry has turned increasingly introspective. Rendered in Spencer’s unmistakable, densely textured brushwork, the tall structure in the middleground rises against a luminous patchwork of sky, its surfaces dissolving gently into light. The crisp delineation that marked his earlier work gives way here to a more atmospheric approach: forms blur, shadows soften, and the entire composition settles into a quiet, almost dreamlike haze. This shift reflects Spencer’s growing tendency in his final years to imagine towns and landscapes rather than depict them directly from observation, lending Peninsula a contemplative, ethereal quality that stands apart from his more bustling earlier scenes.

The rugged waterfront—strewn with stone, debris, and only the faintest traces of human presence—speaks to Spencer’s enduring attachment to the river towns of Pennsylvania. Yet unlike works such as Wharves (1925) or Harlem River (1930), this cityscape feels deserted. The rare figures that remain are small and understated, absorbed into their surroundings and nearly dissolving into them, heightening the mood of hushed isolation. The distant city, barely sketched along the horizon, reinforces this sense of separation from the world beyond, echoing the suggestion of solitude already embedded in the title. Even the central building, with its hollowed windows, appears abandoned. Rather than documenting activity, Spencer turns inward, meditating on the fragile threshold between the built world and nature, and on the quiet poetry of places suspended between permanence and decay.

Through its harmonious blend of structural solidity and painterly dissolution, this late work embodies Spencer’s deeply personal, poetic vision of everyday spaces. Seen in the context of the artist’s final years (when the artist grappled with the evolving language of Modernism as well as profound challenges in his personal life) the work also seems to carry the role of an introspective self-portrait, imbued with the melancholy that characterizes the closing chapter of both his career and life.
